title: A Theravada day
hookLine: chanting, the alms round, sitting, walking, sharing merit

lines: A WOODEN BELL IN THE DARK.
cards: A wooden bell, struck slowly, then faster, in the dark. A forest monastery in northeast Thailand, hours before sunrise. Somewhere a gecko answers.
Monks come down the paths from their huts with flashlights, and the hall fills with Pali chanting. By the time the sky turns gray, they're walking barefoot into the village with their bowls.
For two weeks this path has looked at the way of the elders from the outside. Today: one whole day from the inside, and what its shape is for.

teach.b: The day opens with chanting. Homage first, the line you learned in the practices camp, "Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa": homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened.
Then the refuges, and verses on the qualities of the Buddha, the teaching and the community.
Then the alms round, the pindapata. The monks walk in a line, eyes down, and people wait by the road with rice. Nobody asks.
Nobody haggles. Food goes into the bowl, the giver may bow, and the monk moves on.
Back at the monastery comes the meal, taken before noon, and then the long middle of the day: sitting, walking meditation on a cleared lane, sweeping leaves, sewing, study, a talk from the teacher.
Threaded through it all is the sharing of merit.

When lay people offer food, the monks chant a blessing, and the givers slowly pour water from a small vessel into a bowl, letting the good of the gift flow out to their dead and to all beings. Why this shape?
Each part trains the others. Chanting sets the mind. The alms round keeps monks humble and villagers generous.
Sitting and walking turn calm into seeing. Sharing keeps the good from becoming a private bank account. Now look back at two weeks with the elders.
The way of the elders. Three baskets. The forest remembers.
Rules as a shelter. Two wings. See clearly.
Rising, falling. A map, not a scoreboard. Entering the stream.
Give and receive. For a while. The question is still open.

how: In Theravada monasteries the day usually runs from pre-dawn chanting to the alms round, a meal before noon, sitting and walking meditation, chores and evening chanting; lay people offer food and often pour water while the monks chant, sharing the merit with the dead and all beings.

o: the good that grows from giving and practice
luck earned by lighting candles at a temple
a reward the monks hand out for donations

games.q: match each part of the elders' day.

s: on the alms round, monks ask people for food
they walk in silence with their bowls; people who wish to give are waiting.
lay people often pour water while monks chant a blessing
the water flowing out pictures the merit flowing out to the dead and to all beings.
in a Theravada monastery the day's meal comes before noon
monks keep the rule of not eating after midday.

games.q: you've just offered rice to a line of monks at dawn. later, at the temple, you're handed a small vessel of water while they chant. what's it for?
o: to pour slowly while the merit is shared.
games.why: the pouring pictures the good of the gift flowing out to one's dead and to all beings, so it doesn't stay private.

practice: Here's the day in miniature: if you like, bow once toward whatever you use as a shrine, or just toward the room, then take three slow steps, feeling each foot lift and land. Sit, and let the breath be your whole task.
At the end, silently let whatever good came from it go out to someone who has died, and then to everyone; on a slower day, these four steps can fill fifteen minutes.

wordCard.voice: Puñña. Merit: the good that grows from giving, virtue and meditation, shared and never kept as a private trophy.

orig.note: Pali puñña: merit, the good that grows from giving, virtue and meditation, which Theravada Buddhists share with others.

carryVoice: Your line: the elders' day. Each part trains the others. Tomorrow, the roof of the world.

sources.ref: Khuddakapatha 7, Tirokudda Sutta (giving for the departed)
Vinaya, Pacittiya 37 (not eating at the wrong time)
